incidents.title: Payment API delays checkout
incidents.brief: The checkout endpoint calls a payment provider synchronously and waits on every call.
incidents.constraint: The dependency is slow and thread-blocking.
incidents.question: What makes request latency recover?

choices.label: Deploy Asynchronous Message Broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ) with decoupled worker pool
choices.resultBody: Enqueueing payment jobs via Kafka acknowledges the client in 15ms. Background workers drain the queue at a sustainable rate, shielding client-facing API threads from downstream vendor latency.

choices.label: Increase HTTP client socket timeout to 60s hoping the third-party payment vendor catches up
choices.resultBody: Increasing timeouts keeps HTTP worker threads locked on TCP sockets. Under high concurrency, connection pools starve and cascade 504 Gateway Timeouts to all customer requests.

choices.label: Scale out synchronous API server pods horizontally from 4 to 24 instances
choices.resultBody: Adding more stateless servers merely shifts thread starvation. Each new pod still locks its worker threads on the unresponsive third-party API, increasing cloud costs by 6x without resolving client latency.

hints: The request path is waiting on slow work.
Users only need an ack now.
Enqueue and return.

incidents.title: Email sends hang the request path
incidents.brief: Emails are sent during signup and each request waits for SMTP completion.
incidents.constraint: External email sending is slow and often unreliable.
incidents.question: What should happen after the user account is created?

choices.label: Offload SMTP transmission to background queue (Celery/BullMQ) and return 202 Accepted
choices.resultBody: Offloading email dispatch to background workers returns immediate response to users. SMTP network latency and retries are isolated from the web request loop.

choices.label: Synchronously wait for remote mail relay SMTP handshake and 250 OK before responding to client
choices.resultBody: Synchronous SMTP handshakes across the public internet tie up API worker threads for seconds, causing request queues to back up and p95 latency to explode.

choices.label: Spawn an unmanaged, unmonitored background goroutine/thread inside the web server process
choices.resultTitle: Silent Task Loss on Server Restart
choices.resultBody: Unmanaged in-process threads are immediately killed when the container autoscales or restarts, silently losing user emails without retry mechanisms.

incidents.title: Thumbnails generate too slowly
incidents.brief: Users upload photos and the app renders thumbnails inline in the request path.
incidents.constraint: Thumbnail generation is slow and deferrable.
incidents.question: What is the correct design?

choices.label: Queue upload keys in SQS and resize on a dedicated worker fleet
choices.resultBody: Heavy image transcoding is isolated onto dedicated worker nodes with autoscaling, keeping the web API fleet responsive and healthy.

choices.label: Resize 4K images synchronously on the web API servers before responding
choices.resultBody: Synchronous CPU-intensive image resizing pins CPU cores to 100%, causing Node/Go event loops to stall and dropping concurrent user connections.

choices.label: Have browsers generate every thumbnail variant client-side with Canvas
choices.resultBody: Pushing the work to client devices drains mobile batteries, produces inconsistent thumbnail quality across browsers, and exposes upload endpoints to abuse.

incidents.title: Pay later crash
incidents.brief: A worker crashes after charging a card but before acknowledging the message.
incidents.constraint: The queue may redeliver the same job.
incidents.question: How do you avoid charging twice?

choices.label: Enforce unique Idempotency Keys across payment retries via Redis distributed set
choices.resultTitle: Zero Double Billing on Worker Retries
choices.resultBody: Idempotency keys ensure redelivered payment tasks are recognized and deduplicated, guaranteeing customers are charged exactly once.

choices.label: Disable message redelivery and drop unacknowledged transactions upon worker crash
choices.resultBody: Disabling redeliveries drops customer orders permanently whenever a worker dies mid-flight, causing severe financial and inventory discrepancies.

choices.label: Rely on client users manually noticing failure and retrying payments in the UI
choices.resultBody: Users who receive a timeout error click 'Pay' multiple times, resulting in multiple charges and massive support ticket volume.

incidents.title: Flash sale on the checkout system
incidents.brief: Payment, email, and order processing happen inside the request while the sale peaks.
incidents.constraint: Downstream dependencies are slow and the pool is exhausting threads.
incidents.question: What is the right architectural move?

choices.label: Buffer orders in Kafka and drain at a rate the DB can absorb
choices.resultBody: The queue buffers 50,000 flash sale requests per second and workers write to PostgreSQL at a sustainable 2,500 writes/sec, preventing DB connection pool crashes.

choices.label: Autoscale API containers to 500 pods writing straight to Postgres
choices.resultBody: 500 API pods open thousands of direct database connections, exhausting Postgres max_connections and crashing the entire database cluster.

choices.label: Extend the client and load balancer timeouts to 3 minutes
choices.resultBody: Extended timeouts cause thousands of connections to accumulate at the load balancer, exhausting reverse proxy sockets and bringing down the domain.

incidents.title: Background workers back up
incidents.brief: The queue is growing and workers are falling behind under a sudden spike.
incidents.constraint: Work is queueing faster than it can be processed.
incidents.question: What should be added to prevent collapse?

choices.label: Bound the queue with 429 backpressure and a dead-letter queue
choices.resultBody: Limiting queue capacity prevents broker out-of-memory crashes while backpressure signals clients to slow down, maintaining system stability.

choices.label: Requeue failed jobs instantly without backoff or jitter
choices.resultBody: Retrying failing tasks without backoff creates a retry storm that starves healthy jobs and locks all background workers in continuous failure loops.

choices.label: Auto-ack messages on receipt, before processing completes
choices.resultBody: Auto-acknowledging messages removes them from the broker before execution; if a worker crashes during processing, the task is lost forever.

incidents.title: Complex order processing
incidents.brief: After a user places an order, the platform calculates taxes, emits notifications, and updates a ledger.
incidents.constraint: These steps do not need to complete before the user receives confirmation.
incidents.question: How should the order flow be modeled?

choices.label: Orchestrate multi-step order workflow via Saga Pattern with asynchronous queue checkpoints
choices.resultBody: Decoupling order validation, billing, and fulfillment into sequential asynchronous queue topics provides fault tolerance and compensation checkpoints.

choices.label: Execute inventory reservation, billing, fraud check, and logistics in a single 15-second monolithic web request
choices.resultBody: Chaining multiple slow synchronous HTTP calls inside a single user request causes high failure rates whenever any single downstream dependency lags.

choices.label: Coordinate multi-service order workflow using distributed Two-Phase Commit (2PC) with global locks
choices.resultBody: Synchronous 2PC locks resources across microservices for seconds; coordinator failures leave database rows locked indefinitely.

hints: The request path is waiting on slow work.
Users only need an ack now.
Enqueue and return.

incidents.title: Queue message duplication
incidents.brief: A message is processed twice because a worker crashes before acknowledging it.
incidents.constraint: At-least-once delivery is expected.
incidents.question: What safety property must the job handler provide?

choices.label: Store processed message IDs with a unique constraint; skip repeats
choices.resultBody: Checking message deduplication IDs before processing guarantees at-least-once queue delivery does not cause duplicate side effects.

choices.label: Disable queue redeliveries so a message can never arrive twice
choices.resultTitle: Critical Order Loss on Network Glitches
choices.resultBody: Disabling retries turns reliable delivery into at-most-once delivery, dropping orders whenever temporary network blips occur.

choices.label: Switch consumers to auto-ack so each message is delivered once
choices.resultBody: Auto-ack removes each message the moment it is delivered, so a worker that crashes mid-job loses it for good. Duplicates drop, but at-least-once has quietly become at-most-once.

incidents.title: User places order but waits too long
incidents.brief: The order request waits for analytics, tax calculation, and three downstream APIs before returning a response.
incidents.constraint: Only the order status is needed immediately.
incidents.question: How do you improve user experience without losing correctness?

choices.label: Return 202 with the order ID and push status over WebSockets
choices.resultBody: Returning an immediate 202 Accepted frees the user browser while background workers process the order and push completion status via WebSockets.

choices.label: Keep the spinner until payment, warehouse, tax and tracking APIs finish
choices.resultBody: Synchronously waiting on 4 third-party APIs guarantees p99 response times above 10 seconds, frustrating users and causing duplicate orders.

choices.label: Commit the order locally and skip payment and stock checks
choices.resultBody: Accepting orders blindly creates thousands of unfulfillable commitments that must be refunded manually at significant cost.

hints: The request path is waiting on slow work.
Users only need an ack now.
Enqueue and return.

incidents.title: Crashes during message processing
incidents.brief: A worker starts processing a message, fails mid-way, and the queue redelivers it.
incidents.constraint: The side effect is not safe to repeat unless designed carefully.
incidents.question: What must you design for?

choices.label: Ack only after the DB commit, with idempotent state transitions
choices.resultBody: Acknowledging messages only after the local ACID commit ensures that crashed workers trigger safe re-delivery to surviving nodes.

choices.label: Auto-ack each message on dequeue so crashes never redeliver
choices.resultBody: If a worker crashes while executing an auto-acked message, the message is already gone from the broker and cannot be recovered.

choices.label: Catch handler exceptions and ack the failed message to skip it
choices.resultBody: Silently swallowing exceptions prevents on-call engineers from detecting systemic downstream outages and customer data corruption.

hints: The request path is waiting on slow work.
Users only need an ack now.
Enqueue and return.

incidents.title: Webhook fan-out blocks the API
incidents.brief: A billing service calls 12 partner webhooks inside the same HTTP handler.
incidents.constraint: Partners are slow and sometimes unreachable.
incidents.question: How do you isolate partner latency?

choices.label: Publish webhook events to Kafka and deliver them from a worker pool
choices.resultBody: Webhooks are broadcast through Kafka and dispatched by dedicated egress workers, preventing external partner outages from slowing down the primary API.

choices.label: Call all 12 partner webhooks concurrently in the HTTP handler
choices.resultTitle: API still waits on the slowest partner
choices.resultBody: Concurrent calls cut the sum to the maximum, but every request still waits for the slowest partner, and an unreachable one holds each billing call until its timeout fires.

choices.label: Drop any partner webhook that takes longer than 200 ms to respond
choices.resultBody: Dropping webhooks under load violates API developer contracts and causes partner inventory and billing systems to fall out of sync.

incidents.title: Poison message stalls the queue
incidents.brief: One malformed payload crashes every worker that touches it, so the queue never drains.
incidents.constraint: Later valid jobs are stuck behind the bad one.
incidents.question: What failure-handling pattern unblocks the line?

choices.label: Move a payload to a dead-letter queue after 3 failed attempts
choices.resultBody: Moving malformed payloads to a Dead Letter Queue preserves healthy message flow for remaining customers while alerting engineers for offline inspection.

choices.label: Retry the malformed payload with backoff until it parses
choices.resultBody: Retrying an unparseable payload in an infinite loop blocks the entire queue partition, preventing millions of valid messages from being processed.

choices.label: Halt the worker fleet on any unhandled exception until someone looks
choices.resultBody: Terminating the worker fleet turns an individual bad payload into a complete system-wide processing blackout.

hints: The request path is waiting on slow work.
Users only need an ack now.
Enqueue and return.

incidents.title: Each upload is transcoded four times
incidents.brief: Reelcut transcodes run about 8 minutes, but the SQS visibility timeout is 30 seconds. Messages reappear mid-job, so each video is picked up by ~4 workers. The fleet is at 96% CPU on 2,000 uploads an hour.
incidents.constraint: A crashed worker's job must be retried within 2 minutes.
incidents.question: How do you stop healthy jobs from being redelivered?

choices.label: Heartbeat visibility extensions while each job runs
choices.resultTitle: Jobs stay hidden while they're alive
choices.resultBody: Workers call ChangeMessageVisibility every 60 seconds to push the timeout 2 minutes out. A running job stays invisible for as long as it takes, and a crashed worker stops the heartbeat, so its job reappears within 2 minutes. Fleet CPU falls from 96% to 30%.

choices.label: Triple the transcode worker fleet to clear the backlog
choices.resultTitle: More workers, more copies of each job
choices.resultBody: The extra workers pick up the reappearing messages faster, so each video is now transcoded 6 or 7 times. The bill triples and CPU stays at 90%.

choices.label: Raise the SQS visibility timeout to 12 hours per message
choices.resultBody: Duplicate work stops, but when a worker is killed its video stays hidden for 12 hours before anyone retries it. Spot-instance reclaims strand about 40 uploads a day, far past the 2-minute retry rule.

hints: Compare the job's duration with how long a received message stays hidden.
The queue assumes a worker is dead once the timeout expires.
A live worker can tell the queue it is still working.

incidents.title: SMS provider rejects 93% of welcome texts
incidents.brief: Hatch's TV ad brought 600 signups/s for 5 minutes. Welcome-SMS workers autoscaled to 200 and sent 1,400 req/s against a 100 msg/s provider limit; 93% got HTTP 429 and were retried immediately.
incidents.constraint: The provider limit is per account; a higher tier takes two weeks to approve. Welcome texts may arrive up to an hour late.
incidents.question: How do you get all 180,000 texts delivered without hammering the provider?

choices.label: Cap all SMS workers at 90 sends/s with a shared token bucket
choices.resultBody: A token bucket in Redis lets all workers together send 90 messages per second, just under the limit. The 180,000 texts drain in about 33 minutes, inside the one-hour allowance, with zero 429s. Cost: late signups wait up to half an hour for their text.

choices.label: Spread sends across five more provider API keys in rotation
choices.resultBody: The limit is per account, not per key. The extra keys look like limit evasion, the provider suspends sending for 24 hours, and now every text fails, including login codes.

choices.label: Drop welcome texts that have waited more than 60 seconds
choices.resultTitle: The backlog vanishes, so do the texts
choices.resultBody: The queue empties quickly because most messages are discarded, and workers still retry immediately and still exceed the limit. About 160,000 new users never receive their welcome code.

hints: The provider's limit is lower than the rate the workers are sending at.
The texts have an hour of slack, which is time to spread the work out.
Control the rate at which the whole worker fleet drains the queue.

incidents.title: Carrier recovers, then falls over again
incidents.brief: Parcelly's carrier API was down for 10 minutes, and 400,000 label jobs failed. Workers requeue failures instantly, so on recovery the carrier took 40,000 req/s against a normal 2,000 and crashed again, three times.
incidents.constraint: Labels must print before the 17:00 pickup, about 2 hours away.
incidents.question: How should failed jobs be retried so the carrier can recover?

choices.label: Exponential backoff with full jitter per redelivery
choices.resultTitle: Retries spread out as the carrier recovers
choices.resultBody: Each retry waits a random time between 0 and min(10 min, 2 s x 2^attempt). The 400,000 jobs arrive spread over time instead of together, the carrier stays up at about 3,000 req/s, and the backlog clears in roughly 40 minutes.

choices.label: Wait a fixed 30 seconds before every retry
choices.resultBody: Every failed job waits exactly 30 seconds, so they all come back together. The carrier gets a 40,000 req/s spike every 30 seconds and fails on each one, and the backlog barely shrinks.

choices.label: Send every failed job straight to the dead-letter queue
choices.resultBody: The storm stops, but 400,000 labels now wait for someone to replay the DLQ by hand. A replay all at once would recreate the same spike, so most parcels miss the 17:00 pickup.

hints: Look at when the failed jobs come back.
If every job waits the same amount of time, they still arrive together.
Retry delays should grow and be spread randomly.

incidents.title: Loyalty points credited twice after each deploy
incidents.brief: Orbit Rewards' Kafka consumer credits points in Postgres, then auto-commits offsets every 5 seconds. Each deploy triggers a rebalance, up to 5 seconds of events are consumed again, and about 18,000 purchases get double points.
incidents.constraint: Kafka transactions cannot cover the Postgres write; points must be credited exactly once per purchase.
incidents.question: How do you make a replayed event leave points unchanged?

choices.label: Save consumer offsets in the same DB transaction as points
choices.resultBody: Each batch updates balances and writes the partition's offset in one Postgres transaction. After a rebalance the consumer seeks to the stored offset, so a replayed event is either already committed with its offset or not applied at all. Double credits drop to 0 at the cost of ~2 ms per batch.

choices.label: Enable the Kafka idempotent producer on the checkout service
choices.resultTitle: Fixes duplicates on the wrong side
choices.resultBody: The idempotent producer stops checkout from writing the same event twice to the log. These duplicates come from the consumer reading events again after a rebalance, so every deploy still double-credits about 18,000 purchases.

choices.label: Commit consumer offsets to Kafka before processing each batch
choices.resultBody: This is at-most-once delivery: if a consumer dies after committing but before writing, those events are skipped for good. Double credits stop, but about 11,000 purchases per deploy now get no points at all.

hints: Kafka offsets and the Postgres write are committed separately.
A crash between the two either repeats or skips the work.
Make the record of what was processed part of the same commit as the effect.

incidents.title: Password resets wait 45 minutes behind a newsletter
incidents.brief: Mailroom sends password-reset emails through the same SQS queue as bulk mail. A customer just imported a 3-million-recipient newsletter, and at 1,100 sends/s every reset email now waits about 45 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Reset and 2FA emails must arrive within 30 seconds; the email provider caps you at 1,500 sends/s.
incidents.question: How do you get urgent emails out while the import drains?

choices.label: Separate transactional queue with its own reserved workers
choices.resultTitle: Urgent mail skips the bulk line
choices.resultBody: Resets and 2FA codes go to their own queue with 5 dedicated workers and 200 sends/s of the provider budget. They arrive in about 4 seconds, while bulk mail drains at 1,300 sends/s, about 38 minutes, behind them.

choices.label: Double the shared worker pool from 30 to 60 workers
choices.resultTitle: The provider cap sets the speed
choices.resultBody: Throughput can only reach the 1,500 sends/s provider cap, so the 3 million bulk emails still take 33 minutes. Every reset still waits behind them, now for about 33 minutes instead of 45.

choices.label: Tag each reset email with a high-priority SQS message attribute
choices.resultBody: An SQS standard queue returns messages in roughly arrival order no matter what attributes they carry. Workers only see the priority after receiving the message, so resets still wait about 45 minutes behind the import.

hints: Adding workers doesn't help when urgent messages are in line behind millions of others.
The queue has no way to put one message ahead of another.
Different latency requirements call for different lines.

incidents.title: Paid orders never reach the warehouse
incidents.brief: Freshbox's order handler commits to Postgres, then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka. When a pod dies between the two steps, from OOM kills or deploys, the event is lost. Last week 1,140 paid orders never shipped.
incidents.constraint: The warehouse must only ever see orders that were actually committed.
incidents.question: How do you guarantee every committed order produces its event?

choices.label: Write the event to an outbox table in the order's transaction
choices.resultTitle: The event commits with the order
choices.resultBody: The order row and its outbox row commit together or not at all. A relay (Debezium reading the WAL) publishes outbox rows to Kafka and marks them sent, so a crash only delays an event. Missing orders drop to 0. Cost: delivery is at-least-once, so the warehouse consumer must dedupe by order ID.

choices.label: Publish OrderPlaced to Kafka before committing the order
choices.resultTitle: Events for orders that never existed
choices.resultBody: Lost events stop, but 3% of orders roll back after publishing, for example on failed fraud checks. The warehouse now packs about 820 boxes a week for orders that were never committed.

choices.label: Retry the Kafka publish three times in the request handler
choices.resultTitle: Retries don't survive a dead pod
choices.resultBody: Retries cover brief broker errors, but an OOM-killed or redeployed pod never runs its retry loop. Missing orders fall only from 1,140 to about 700 a week, and slow retries add 50 ms to p95.

hints: Two separate systems are written one after the other with no shared commit.
Changing the order of the two writes changes which failure you get.
Make the event part of the same database write as the order.

incidents.title: Telemetry broker nears its memory alarm
incidents.brief: Pulsegrid devices publish 8,000 events/s to RabbitMQ. Consumers insert one row and commit per message, topping out at 5,000/s with Postgres at 90% CPU. The queue grows by 3,000/s and broker memory is at 88%.
incidents.constraint: Telemetry must not be dropped, and Postgres cannot be upgraded this month.
incidents.question: How do you make consumers keep up before the broker blocks publishers?

choices.label: Consume in batches of 500 with one bulk INSERT per batch
choices.resultBody: Consumers prefetch 500 messages, write them with one multi-row INSERT, then ack the batch. Per-commit overhead is paid once per 500 rows, so throughput reaches about 25,000 rows/s at 40% Postgres CPU and the backlog drains in minutes. Cost: a crash replays up to 500 events, so inserts use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.

choices.label: Raise the broker's memory high-watermark to 95% of RAM
choices.resultTitle: A few more minutes before the alarm
choices.resultBody: Consumers are still 3,000 events/s behind, so the extra headroom fills within minutes. Then the alarm blocks every publisher, devices buffer and drop data, and the broker is left too close to its OOM limit.

choices.label: Cap the queue at 1M messages with drop-head overflow
choices.resultBody: The broker stays healthy by discarding the oldest messages, 3,000 every second, which breaks the no-drop rule. Consumer throughput is still stuck at 5,000/s.

hints: The queue grows because consumers are slower than producers.
Measure the cost of each database commit, not each row.
Do more work per round-trip to Postgres.

incidents.title: Hotel fails, traveller keeps a flight they didn't want
incidents.brief: Wanderly books flight, then hotel, then car through a queue-driven workflow. When the hotel step fails (4% of trips, mostly sold out), nothing undoes the flight. 600 travellers a week are charged for stranded flights.
incidents.constraint: Partner APIs are plain REST; they support book and cancel, but no prepare/commit.
incidents.question: How do you leave no half-booked trips when a later step fails?

choices.label: Run compensating cancels in reverse order, retried until done
choices.resultTitle: Every completed step can be undone
choices.resultBody: The orchestrator records each finished step. On failure it enqueues cancel-car, cancel-hotel and cancel-flight for completed steps, newest first, retried with backoff and keyed by booking reference so a repeated cancel is harmless. Stranded flights drop to 0. Cost: some fares carry a cancellation fee, which the business absorbs.

choices.label: Wrap the flight, hotel and car calls in a two-phase commit
choices.resultBody: 2PC needs every participant to support prepare and commit. The airline and hotel APIs only book or cancel, so the coordinator can't hold a booking in a prepared state and trips still end half-booked.

choices.label: Keep retrying the failed hotel booking with backoff until it books
choices.resultBody: Most failures are sold-out rooms, so retries never succeed. Trips sit in 'pending' for hours while the flight is already charged, and 540 travellers a week still end up with a flight and no hotel.

hints: One step already changed the outside world before the failure.
Distributed transactions need partner support that isn't there.
For every forward step, define the step that undoes it.

incidents.title: Resize workers OOM-killed mid-job every six hours
incidents.brief: Snapcase's resize workers leak about 300 MB an hour since image-lib 4.2. Each hits its 2 GB limit after roughly six hours and is OOM-killed mid-job; 3% of 1,800 jobs/hour get redelivered late.
incidents.constraint: The upstream leak fix ships Thursday, three days out; jobs are idempotent and workers drain cleanly on SIGTERM.
incidents.question: What keeps jobs finishing cleanly until the fix ships?

choices.label: Rolling-restart workers every 4 hours until the patch ships
choices.resultTitle: Workers recycle before the leak bites
choices.resultBody: A scheduled rolling restart sends SIGTERM to one worker at a time every 4 hours; each finishes its current job, exits and returns with a clean heap. Peak memory stays near 1.3 GB, OOM kills stop and redeliveries fall to 0.1%. Cost: one cron job to delete on Thursday.

choices.label: Dead-letter any job whose worker died twice while running it
choices.resultTitle: Healthy jobs pile up in the DLQ
choices.resultBody: These jobs aren't poison; the leak kills whichever job happens to be running when memory runs out. About 50 valid resizes a day land in the dead-letter queue and need a manual replay, and the OOM kills continue every six hours.

choices.label: Split each resize into checkpointed steps on separate queues
choices.resultTitle: A week of work for a three-day bug
choices.resultBody: Checkpoints would let a killed job resume from its last step, but the rewrite takes longer than Thursday's fix, adds three queues to operate, and the workers keep leaking and getting OOM-killed every six hours meanwhile.

hints: Ask when this problem goes away on its own.
Memory climbs steadily and resets whenever a process starts fresh.
Jobs are idempotent and workers drain on SIGTERM, so stopping one is cheap.
